cells.tense: The steadying is happening here, in your own hands, and it's steady today.
cells.ask: Name one thing this week you're keeping going — one sentence, written or out loud — and notice whose it is.
cells.core:
The steadying is coming from you, and it works because it's even, not because it's loud. You're in the room where you get to be what you are, and the people you do this for can feel it without being told.

That steadiness is a working floor, not a diploma. Next to it there's a stretch where it could be building something it hasn't tried yet — the same warmth feeding what you actually want to see happen. One sentence, one name for what you're holding up, costs nothing and proves you can say it without flinching. It can hand back a clearer picture of what the fire is for, and where it wants to go next.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping it steady, and it's your hand on it.
cells.verb: keeping the fire warm and steady — holding momentum, courage, and other people's will to keep going, without burning out
cells.place: the place where you become what you already are — nothing dimmed, nothing distorted, nothing borrowed

cells.tense: The steadying has already left now — it's out ahead, bracing against a next thing you can't write in yet.
cells.ask: Write down the next thing you're pushing — then park it for a day and check it against what's actually true.
cells.core:
You're carrying momentum nobody asked you to carry, and the planning has momentum of its own — you're three scenes ahead and the third one is the one running you. Steering like that makes you the last one to feel the road, and the pace you're setting has stopped being yours.

The steadying that works here asks before it pushes: it holds still, checks the ground, then earns its pace. Pulling the next thing back a beat isn't losing the plot — the plot goes on, just not from the back of a horse you haven't saddled. A day's pause tells you which of your speeds is real. It can hand back traction: the direction you can actually walk at instead of the one you're braced against.

cells.tense: The steadying is behind you now — you're standing past the door where you used to keep the fire open.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been keeping alive past its time, and this week do the single act that ends it.
cells.core:
Kept well, this is what it looks like: you know which fires are yours to hold, you feed them on purpose, and you let the rest go dark without apologizing. The people you keep warm can tell you're there. You stop paying for things that already ended.

What's happening instead is that the fuel ran out a while back and the keeping-hold kept going. Ending something isn't capricious — it's choosing where the last of it goes. Naming what you'll stop holding isn't giving up; endings handled like that tend to bring the rest back with them, and every clean finish buys something. One thing, ended this week, is what steadies the part of you running on nothing.

cells.tense: The steadying is running right now and it's already shaped like something — you just haven't signed it.
cells.ask: Write the first line of the next chapter yourself — in your own words, on actual paper — and start from there.
cells.core:
Something is already happening here and the source isn't luck — it's you, keeping the direction, holding the line, doing the work. Call it how-it's-gone, call it whatever ships. But if you left the room the direction would notice, which is one of the most grounded proofs there is.

Setting the shape before you push — one line, in your own hand, no permission asked — doesn't ask you to make the case, just to take the pen. That belongs to the sitting-still kind of beginning, the one that makes the rest less breaking and more direction you meant. Putting the line on paper makes the next one easier to walk. It's already yours; that's what it hands back.

attempts.check: The riskiest claim is in the Balanced core: that the keeping is being chosen rather than just happening — the record says the capacity is operating well, but an unexamined habit can look identical from outside, so I've put the choice in a person's own hands ('It's yours') and offered an experiment they can refuse rather than asserting inner awareness. A reader could reasonably say the fire kept warm here is other people's, not their own — so every cell keeps the object of the keeping unspecified and the ask doable in whatever they're actually tending. Each ask survives a wrong read: naming one thing you're keeping going, tuning one plan against what's true, letting one ending land, and writing your own first line all teach the person something whether or not the map was right about them; the sentence that served the writer most was an early 'the fire doesn't need you to hold your breath' — cut, too picture-perfect.
